memory_candidates.content: A shell test suite that resolves a sibling script belonging to a DIFFERENT extension (e.g. a lean-owned test invoking core's verify-lean-mcp.sh) must not hardcode a single SCRIPT_DIR-relative path. The source store keeps extensions in separate directory trees (lean/scripts/tests/../../../core/scripts/foo.sh), but deploy flattens every extension's scripts into one .claude/scripts/ directory, making the sibling one level up instead (scripts/tests/../foo.sh). Try both candidate paths in order (source-store form, then deployed-tree form) so the same suite runs identically pre- and post-deploy -- caught by actually re-deploying to a consumer repo and re-running the suite there, not merely by running it in the source tree.

In a bash test harness, do not capture a called function's side-effect variable (e.g. an exit-code global set via `$?` inside the function) through command substitution: `OUT="$(fn ...)"` runs fn in a subshell, so any variable it sets is discarded when the subshell exits, producing an unbound-variable error under `set -u` on the next read. Fix: have the function write its captured stdout+stderr to a caller-supplied output file and run it directly in the current shell (no `$()` wrapper) so `$?`/the side-effect variable is read immediately in the parent shell; read the file separately for the content.

For a hot-path preflight check wrapping an existing diagnostic script with strict exit codes, prefer WARN-always-exit-0 over propagating the underlying tool's exit code as a block, when the degraded mode remains usable (e.g. lean4 work without lean-lsp still works via compiled probes, just slower). Make the WARN actionable (name the exact remedy command) rather than a bare mismatch report -- an unactionable warning is functionally equivalent to no warning, which is the original defect this pattern exists to fix. Distinguish semantically different non-zero exit codes in the message (e.g. 'currently indexes a different project' vs 'misregistered') so operators don't learn to ignore the check.
